doc.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Cincinnati bands, race and the road to college
title: His birthday and a shared connection with Coltrane
summary: Both born on September 23, Foster says his style resembled Coltrane's until Trane joined Miles and he joined Basie.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Well we can stop there, because first of all, happy birthday.
We should say for the record, this is taking place on the day after your 70th.
And I wondered, and this is a real digression, is there some connection? I mean do you feel a connection with Coltrane? Does the 23rd -- does that day -- does that mean something to you?
Definitely. I feel a connection -- there’s a fact that in although we’re two years apart, he having been born in 1926. Before he joined -- was it with Monk first or Miles?
I think it was Miles first. I think it was Miles, Monk, Miles.

Miles, Monk, Miles, yeah. Before his first tour of duty with Miles, his style and my style were very similar. This is around 1954, I think, ’55. I remember hearing a recording of his and I remember remarking to myself, wow, he sounds a lot like me. Then he got with Miles and I with Basie, and our paths went in vastly different directions. Trying to fit with the Basie orchestra and being torn between the Lester Young approach, and the Buddy Tate, Don Byas approach, and really being in love with Sonny Stitt, I was all kind of messed up, while Trane, his direction was very definite and intense. Here I -- while I’m trying to fit with this institution, long-standing institution, by veering back and forth between Prez and Don Byas and Buddy Tate, my style became diffused, whereas Trane was pinpointed in a certain direction. Then he left me in the lurch.
I don’t know about that, but that’s -­
Because this confusion lasted a number of years until I decided, hey, I’m going for myself.
